properties.c_notes:
Tomb 3 is a chamber tomb cut into the tuff and strongly truncated by ploughing, preserving a shallow chamber and a reduced entrance/threshold zone (with a step/downward transition into the cell). The fill is compact and the anthropolical material is fragmentary: teeth and traces of skeletal remains suggest a young adult, with limited grave goods (small quantities of pottery and lithics). 

Tomb 3 produced charcoal/wood fragments identified as alder (Alnus) and maple (Acer). A separate radiocarbon measurement is reported from an oak (Quercus) charcoal sample taken from this tomb (OxA-8078: 3990±55 BP; cal. 2720–2490 BC), linking Tomb 3 securely to the later 3rd millennium BC (Copper Age).

Bibliography: Anzidei et al., La necropoli eneolitica di Lunghezzina (Roma) (2003); Anzidei e Carboni 2020, "Roma prima del mito".

properties.c_notes:
In the Lunghezzina cemetery, Tomb 8 stands out for its preservation and stratigraphic potential. It is a chamber tomb with part of the vault surviving, and a vestibule described as semi-lunar and sloping toward the chamber. The structure yielded clear evidence relevant to closure practices and “threshold activity” (including a flint arrowhead interpreted as a possible offering), while differences in sediment between vestibule and chamber were used to argue for controlled access and possible periodic reopening.

It is also the richest context for charcoal macro-remains: anthracological analysis reports ash (Fraxinus sp.) as dominant (dozens of fragments from the cell/vestibule/near the recesses), along with maple (Acer sp.) from the chamber floor and alder (Alnus sp.) from the vestibule. A radiocarbon determination is reported from an ash charcoal sample connected with the door/recess area (LTL2901A: 4100±60 BP; cal. 2890–2620 BC).

Bibliography: Anzidei et al., La necropoli eneolitica di Lunghezzina (Roma) (2003); Anzidei e Carboni 2020, "Roma prima del mito".

properties.c_notes:
Tomb 6 is a relatively better-defined grotticella tomb, with a sub-rectangular vestibule and lateral recesses near the chamber access. Small travertine stones found near the entrance are interpreted not as door-slabs but more plausibly as markers/ritual elements. The chamber yielded little or no in situ human skeletal material in the excavated levels; finds from the fill include small artefacts such as a copper awl, consistent with a funerary assemblage but not particularly rich. 

Botanical macro-remains are especially meaningful here; tomb 6 produced seven charcoal fragments of elm (Ulmus sp.), concentrated in the left lateral recess close to the chamber entrance—a pattern explicitly interpreted as possibly related to a wooden closing device/door rather than casual background charcoal.

Bibliography: Anzidei et al., La necropoli eneolitica di Lunghezzina (Roma) (2003); Anzidei e Carboni 2020, "Roma prima del mito".

properties.c_notes:
Grave 3 belongs to the group of small pit-type graves (3–7) cut into the cocciopesto floor after the main hypogeal/ossuary phase. Grave 3 itself was found intact at discovery and contained multiple inhumations (an adult female c. 20–30 years and two infants), with small personal/devotional items (e.g., textile fragments, rosary parts, a bronze earring, a gold enamelled ring).

The botanical evidence derives primarily from coffin construction: wood traces preserved by “metallization” around iron nails, identified as alder (Alnus sp.), with plank thickness inferred at c. 25–28 mm.

Bibliography: Sadori e Sabato 2009

properties.c_notes:
Grave 6 belongs to the group of small pit-type graves (3–7) cut into the cocciopesto floor after the main hypogeal/ossuary phase. The grave was repeatedly reopened/reused. The final use of Grave 6, along with other tombs of this group, is connected to a phase of repairs/patching in the western aisle (bricks used to plug lacunae), after which a thin cocciopesto layer sealed some graves.

Archaeobotanical evidence comes from the coffin construction: Grave 6 is explicitly grouped with Graves 3 and 5 for the wooden remains preserved on nails, all identified as alder (Alnus sp.), again with consistent board thickness inferred from the nail-associated traces.

properties.c_notes:
Area over roughly 100 m² centered on a large pit whose fills include deposits dated to the 13th century BC. This feature was later re-cut and accompanied by a dump pit, additional pits, and small channels, with later phases extending into the Final Bronze Age. Assemblages from the earlier fills include refined (purified) clay pottery, a copper “cake”/ingot fragment and copper (and lead-related) melting residues, a small number of glass-paste beads, and—crucially—an Aegean-type stirrup-jar handle attributed to Late Helladic IIIB–IIIC, suggesting long-distance connections (with provenance discussed through archaeometric sampling in subsequent work).Published plans exist but do not precisely locate the layout within the overall hill setting; the plan is therefore placed here only approximately (as “W”), while preserving correct dimensions. 

Bibliography: Angle et al. 1993, Casale Nuovo (LT) e la tarda età del bronzo nel Lazio meridionale, pp. 273–274; Alessandri, L. 2008, p. 108

properties.c_notes:
Fieldwork in this area documented c. 25 circular pits on the summit and upper slopes, ranging from small features (c. 50–80 cm in diameter) to larger ones (up to c. 150–200 cm), generally shallow in preserved depth beneath the plough zone. Their fills included ceramics (including “Boschetto”-style decorated cups), calcined animal bone, and blocks of light/reddish sandstone interpreted as tempering material, alongside evidence consistent with craft waste. On this basis, the pits have been interpreted as installations for clay settling/decantation connected with nearby clay sources and ceramic production; minor metallurgical indicators (e.g., copper slag and lead) are also reported from the broader area. All archeobotanical materials comes from one such pit.

The published plans (e.g., Tavv. V–VI) provide the pit layouts but lack a precise georeferenced placement on the hillock; therefore, they are positioned only approximately here (following the E/W distinction) while keeping their internal dimensions correct.

properties.c_notes:
The “Sala dei Sette” is the largest, most accessible chamber in the inner sector of Grotta Vittorio Vecchi and was therefore chosen for stratigraphic investigation. It is a spacious room with niches and dense concentrations of archaeological material, terminating against a major collapse that sealed the ancient entrance. The evidence points to repeated funerary and ritual use, with human remains often clustered along walls and in niches, occasional reworking of older deposits toward the centre, and the presence of a hearth linked to these practices. Fieldwork in and around the chamber was organised through test pits: A2, a long trench along the entrance/collapse, documented a sequence from landslide sealing and water-laid silts to stalagmitic phases and a dark anthropogenic layer rich in Bronze Age materials; A1 sampled this deposit (two spits), yielding later disturbance (including an Archaic bronze fibula) and a hearth above, and denser human remains below (including an inverted bowl covering a child’s skull); A3, between the collapse base and Ambiente A, produced well-preserved pottery (mostly closed forms) and bronze items (e.g., chisel, pin), while Ambiente A yielded in situ bones and the site’s only bronze dagger. Published plans and sections locate the chamber and pits, but as cave-survey drawings without precise georeferencing; GIS placement is therefore approximate, while preserving correct internal proportions. 

Bibliography: Guidi & Rosini, Materiali protostorici dalla grotta Vittorio Vecchi (Sezze Romano, LT).

properties.c_notes:
The remains comes from two specific USS:

US 3096: Structural collapse debris from the kiln’s vault/roof associated with the later installation (US 3006); part of the superstructure failure phase (in tandem with US 3069).

US 3007: descrizione Charred elements of the internal wall framework: ash (Fraxinus) planks and members of deciduous oak, belonging to the inner wall framing of the same kiln phase (US 3006).

The ceramic-production complex identified as probable horizontal kilns, set in a sub-elliptical cavity cut into natural silt and clay, with a concave floor sloping east and side walls lined with large tuff blocks. The sequence shows discontinuous use, with phases separated by sandy abandonment fills. The earliest installation (US 3186) was larger and apsidal; it bears a thick carbonaceous layer overlain by sand lenses and “concotto” lumps, plus strongly altered, vitrified, bubble-marked surfaces indicating temperatures >1000 °C (US 3120), likely from an uncontrolled overheating event that led to abandonment. A subsequent, smaller kiln (US 3006), inserted within the first and sharing its orientation, has a thin carbon layer (US 3097) with charcoal of maple, plum, boxwood, and deciduous oak, along with structural remains from the vault collapse (US 3096, 3069) and the internal wall framework (US 3007). A final, even smaller apsidal structure (UUSS 3037=3041), similarly oriented, occupies the southern portion of the cut.

(bibliography: De Santis et alii 2010, pp. 275-277)

properties.c_notes:
A miniaturized impasto vessel (no. 7) containing charred fragments of evergreen oak and boxwood comes from a large, deep oval well oriented north–south and cut into natural silt and clay. Midway down, the shaft narrowed to a smaller inner pit sealed by hefty blocks of lionato tuff and a quadrangular sandstone slab set horizontally at center. 

On the floor of this inner pit stood a ‘urna a capanna’ (hut-urn) encircled by eight miniaturized impasto vessels. The miniature bronzes comprised a spear with cast shaft placed in front of the urn’s doorway, while inside the urn two pairs of “double shields,” a pair of greaves, and a fibula were laid above the cremated bones, with a fragment of a bronze-sheet knife at the bottom. Abundant faunal remains of caprine and bovine were also preserved.

(bibliography: De Santis et alii 2011, p. 267)

properties.c_notes:
The remains comes from two distint elements:

Vessel 1 — ‘boccale’ (jug): contained charcoal of evergreen oak.

Vessel 7 — ‘poppatoio’ (feeding bottle) with vertical ring handle: contained charcoal of evergreen oak and boxwood.

Small circular ‘pozzetto’, shallow and cut into natural silt and clay. The cover was almost entirely removed; the fill consisted of medium and small blocks of lionato tuff, with an additional travertine crust block to the west. On the floor sat the cinerary urn, closed with an inverted vessel base used as a lid; above it lay the miniaturized grave goods, including items typical of infant burials such as a ‘boccale’ and a ‘poppatoio’. One bowl contained sheep remains; lamb bones were also placed within the cinerary urn. Charred evergreen-oak fragments were found in vessels 1 and 7; boxwood was identified in vessel 7. Anthropology: sub-adult, c. 2 years; sex indeterminate.

Miniaturized impasto set comprising: a ‘boccale’ (1); a ‘scodella’ (2); a ‘piattello troncoconico’ used as the lid of the ‘poppatoio’ (3); a ‘tazzina’ (4; and another small cup, 6); a ‘scodellina carenata’ with horizontal grip (5); a ‘poppatoio’ with vertical ring handle (7); a vessel base reused as the cinerary lid (8); the cinerary urn (9); sheep ribs among the ashes (10).

properties.c_notes: Small, plain-surfaced ovoid olletta with a short flaring neck, from Tomb 2—a shallow, oval cremation pit cut into natural silt and clay and lined, covered, and filled with lionato tuff blocks and earth with traces of charcoal. The cinerary urn with roof lid stood upright at the center; the assemblage was entirely miniaturized. The olletta (no. 6) contained charred boxwood fragments; faunal offerings were placed nearby and in/over vessels 6, 8, and 10. Associated finds include nine impasto vessels concentrated to the west (lamp-tray, small jars—one net-decorated—a boat-shaped vessel, deep cup with over-rising handle, single-handled small bowl, three-footed plate, biconical olletta) and bronzes to the east (serpentine-arch fibula, Celano-type knife, paired “double shields” of sheet bronze with fastening hooks, and a spear). The deceased was a young adult male (c. 20–25 years). Calibrated 14C places the burial in the late Bronze–early Iron Age (ca. 11th–9th century BC).

properties.c_notes:
Seventh-century BC stratigraphic unit characterized by domestic/storage debris: several olle and hearth fittings, plus a small ‘dolio’ packed with charred broad-bean (Vicia faba) seeds—interpretable as a foodstuff deposit. Charcoal is abundant, dominated by evergreen oak (holm/cork oak), with lesser deciduous oak and a trace of boxwood.

(bibliography: de Santis et alii 2010, p. 279)

properties.c_notes:
A partially buried ‘dolio’ with four cylindrical lugs at its maximum girth cuts across the western sector, intersecting the perimeter drain and a hut posthole. It was subsequently scarred by the installation of a fire-related structure (US 3002), in use from the beginning of phase IIIB through the whole IV period, and later by historical works (Caesarian leveling and an early-medieval vine trench). The vessel was likely repurposed as a refuse container: inside were domestic materials—a lid, a cup fragment with an obliquely ribbed shoulder, fragments of hearth/stove fittings, containers for provisions, and a piece of bronze wire with triangular section. Environmental remains included charred caryopses of barley and einkorn (Triticum monococcum), charcoal of Prunus sp. and evergreen oak (holm/cork oak), and very fragmentary animal bones. Within the site sequence, the ‘dolio’ is attributed to phase IIIA, while a nearby infant tomb (Tomb 9) belongs to phases IIIB2/IVA1.

(bibliography: de Santis et alii 2010, pp. 273-274)

properties.c_notes:
A fired-clay ‘piastra di cottura’ dating to the initial phase of Period III (phase IIIA, late 9th century BC) was identified near the southern edge of the excavation. Its surface was later truncated by several large 7th-century BC postholes. From the surrounding context came charred barley caryopses and charcoal of evergreen oak (holm/cork oak), indicating nearby firing and food-processing activities.

(bibliography: de Santis et alii 2010, p.274)

properties.c_notes:
Associated with the Period III–IV occupation in Area B, the well is roughly 0.8 m in diameter and more than 6 m deep. The upper stretch was unlined and equipped with footholds, while the lower shaft was strengthened with small blocks of lionato tuff where the natural deposits are most friable. It was dug through Paleotiber alluvium: clayey silts with pumice lenses near the top, grading into yellowish sands below; the water table lay about 6 m down (c. 8.40 m a.s.l.), and the shaft likely did not continue much beyond that level. 

On the floor were the only two complete (or fully reconstructable) vessels: a locally made globular jug in refined clay with painted bands and oblique motifs, and an imported kotyle datable to Early Protocorinthian (last quarter of the 8th century BC). Interpreted as a drinking set, they were probably placed intentionally when the well was first put into service. The overlying fills contained abundant refuse—table wares (cups, pyxides, red-impasto ollae), cooking pots and trays, storage containers (dolia, cylinder-ovoid ‘ollette’), hearth fittings and two spools—entirely fragmentary and redeposited, indicating dumping after the well fell out of use. The backfill appears to have been a single operation in the early 6th century BC, coinciding with site leveling and a new construction phase. Faunal remains include cattle, caprines, and pigs, as well as at least three juvenile dogs (under one year) bearing butchery and burning marks. Paleobotanical sampling recovered very abundant charred plant remains—grains of barley and wheat and broad-bean seeds—consistent with the contemporary habitation deposits.

(bibliography: de Santis et alii 2010, pp. 279-281)

properties.c_notes:
A narrow, shallow rectangular pit with rounded corners, oriented northwest–southeast and cut into natural silt and clay, was found with its covering entirely removed; the fill consisted of the same sediment. The individual lay supine on the grave floor, head to the northwest, limbs extended, and was likely wrapped in a shroud fastened at the chest and feet. 

The assemblage was limited to personal ornaments: a necklace combining amber discoid beads, glass beads, conical amber buttons, amber pendants, and small gold spirals; multiple fibulae (including a serpentine-arch example with disc foot and several thickened-bow types, one large); a spiral wire hair-fastener; a small bronze wire ring with cylindrical pendants and amber beads; and loose bronze wire with amber fragments. Animal offerings—bovine and caprine remains—were placed near the right femur and behind the skull.

(bibliography: De Santis et alii 2011, p. 268)
properties.bibliography: De Santis, A.,_Mieli, G.,_Rosa, C.,_Matteucci, R.,_Celant, A._2010_Le fasi di occupazione nell'area centrale di Roma in età protostorica: nuovi dati dagli scavi nel Foro di Cesare_Scienze dell'Antichità: 16, 2010_259-284

properties.c_notes:
A truncated-conical 'dolio' with a finger-impressed cordon below the rim was set at the bottom of a circular well cut into natural silt and clay; the shaft, filled and covered with blocks of lionato tuff, narrowed to a smaller pit sealed by a convex tuff block. Inside the 'dolio' stood the cinerary urn (a biconical olla with a horizontal handle and three conical bosses) closed by a conical lid, accompanied by six miniaturized impasto vessels (a three-footed plate/stool, a bowl, three plain 'ollette', and one 'olletta' with inturned rim). 

Miniature bronzes placed among the ashes inside the urn comprised a razor, a serpentine-arch fibula with spiral-disc foot, and a spear with cast shaft; a fragment of another serpentine-arch fibula came from the fill. Charred evergreen-oak wood (holm oak/cork oak) and pig remains were present in the fills. The interred individual was an adult male.

(bibliography: De Santis et alii 2011, p. 266)

properties.c_notes:
A regular rectangular pit with rounded corners, oriented northwest–southeast and cut into natural silt and clay, contained an infant laid supine on the floor of the grave, head to the northwest, limbs extended, the left hand placed beneath the pelvis. The covering was missing; the fill—of the same sediment—yielded a few pottery fragments. The arrangement of skeletal parts observed during excavation suggests the body was wrapped in a binding or shroud. 

The grave goods, all of normal size, comprised two vessels at the feet and a third placed over the pelvis; two spindle whorls near the left femur; ornaments on the chest (small cast rings, an amber pendant, an amber discoid bead, a fibula with thickened bow and three suspension rings, and a necklace of amber discoid beads); a spiral wire hair-fastener beside the right side of the skull; and a cast bronze suspension ring at the feet. Faunal offerings (piglet remains) were set near the knees and the right foot, and charcoal of evergreen oak was present. On the basis of the assemblage, the burial is attributed to a female child aged approximately 4–5 years.

(bibliography: De Santis et alii 2011, p. 269)

properties.context_name: Tomba 1 (Area funeraria dal Foro di Cesare)
properties.c_notes:
A shallow, oval cremation pit oriented east–west was uncovered, its cover and fill—small lionato tuff blocks mixed with earth—partly disturbed. The cinerary urn, laid horizontally with its lid placed beneath, occupied the eastern end, while the grave goods were arranged to the west. The assemblage, entirely miniaturized, comprised impasto pottery (including a biconical olla used as the urn with a roof-shaped lid, small net-decorated jars, a deep cup with a biforate handle, a single-handled bowl, a three-footed plate/stool, two askoi, a small jar with an inturned rim, and a boat-shaped vessel) and a few bronze items, notably “double shields” made from overlapping sheet discs with a central perforation and repoussé decoration, as well as a fragmentary serpentine-arch fibula. Faunal remains of young lambs were also present. Anthropological analysis indicates an adult male, about 30–40 years old. The burial belongs to the early Latial IIA1 horizon (roughly 11th–10th century BC), consistent with calibrated radiocarbon results spanning the later 13th to early 10th centuries BC.

(bibliography: De Santis et alii 2011, p. 264)

properties.chron_orig: second half of the 4th - second half to end of the 5th century AD
properties.c_notes:
In the SW area south-west of the Domus Tiberiana, where service-facing rooms and sanitary/drainage installations played a major role. This area shows a clear imperial development: Domitianic rooms were reorganised in the Hadrianic phase into five vaulted spaces abutting the southern cryptoporticus, including a water container and a latrine, with further sewer-system refurbishments and at least one intervention around the turn of the 3rd–4th century (new branch and new hydraulic flooring).

A Trench cut in the area (Trench W), from wich the botanical samples derive, shows abandonment phases (c. 350–390 AD) affecting the broader complex, followed by a progressive retreat and use as dump in the Late Antiquity phase.
properties.source: Coletti, F. and Celant, A. , 2006, fig. 1

properties.context_name: Aedes Victoriae - Temple of Victory (Trench V)
properties.c_notes:
The Temple of Victory on the south-western Palatine was dedicated in 294 BC by L. Postumius Megellus and stood immediately adjacent to the Temple of Magna Mater, with the small shrine of Victoria Virgo also in the same cluster. Ancient sources and later scholarship emphasise that the building remained an important landmark on the clivus Victoriae, and that it underwent substantial restoration in the late Republican/early Augustan period (perhaps connected with the Palatine fire of AD 3). In wider historical terms, the temple is also functionally intertwined with the Magna Mater sanctuary: traditions record that Cybele’s sacred stone was housed in the Temple of Victory between its arrival in Rome (204 BC) and the dedication of the Magna Mater temple (191 BC), reinforcing the idea of a tightly integrated sacred landscape.

Trench V—from which the botanical samples derive—is explicitly tied to foundation stratigraphy, and is therefore connected with the construction phase (and earliest monumental arrangement) of the Victory complex.
properties.source: Coletti, F. and Celant, A. , 2006, fig. 1
properties.bibliography: Coletti, F.,_Celant, A.,_Pensabene Perez, P._2006_Ricerche archeologiche e paleoambientali sul Palatino tra l’età arcaica e la tardoantichità–primi risultati_Innovazioni tecnologiche per i beni culturali in Italia. Atti del convegno Pàtron_557-564

properties.context_name: Service Quarter of Magna Mater Temple (Late Antiquity)
properties.c_notes: In the western area of the Magna Mater sanctuary stood a service area. The botanical samples derive from a trench (RZ) wich is a reference point for the late sequence of the area, because its deposits capture both restructuring and decline: after earlier imperial arrangements, the sector undergoes a 3rd–4th century AD reorganisation and then a pronounced trajectory of abandonment and secondary use.  Thrench RZ - and the overall area - is then explicitly linked to the mid–late 5th century pattern of sporadic reoccupation as dump/overflow ('inondazione'/'colmata'), before the final collapse dynamics that close the sequence into the early 6th century.
properties.source: Coletti, F. and Celant, A. , 2006, fig. 1

properties.chron_orig: second half of the 4th century AD
properties.c_notes: The West collector belongs to the Colosseum’s drainage network and slopes gradually outward. Investigations begun in 1973 found clear evidence that the conduit became blocked and inactive in the second half of the 4th century AD, preserving a sealed deposit of waste flushed from within the amphitheatre. This waterterlogged sediment trapped a rich assemblage of plant remains (seeds, fruits, leaves) and even a small set of worked wooden objects; the botanical spectrum is consistent with food debris from spectators alongside incidental plant inputs.

properties.chron_orig: second half of the 4th century AD
properties.c_notes:
The East collector was explored during restoration/strengthening works on the amphitheatre foundations, in a broader context where sections of the sewer system had been sealed for roughly 1,600 years. Its sediment is described as largely sandy, with organic plant matter preserved under asphyctic/reducing, waterlogged conditions, allowing recovery (via water-separation) of an unusually “fresh-looking” assemblage. 

The recorded taxa include a wide range of cultivated foods (e.g., vine, fig, olive, nuts, cereals), spices/oil plants, and also ornamental and wild/ruderal species—a combination interpreted as reflecting both consumption inside the amphitheatre and the local vegetation history of the monument’s sealed micro-environment.

properties.c_notes:
Stratigraphic tests carried out along the southern and eastern sides of the Arch of Constantine (notably in the context of restoration-related investigations) show that post-classical deposits are extremely discontinuous in this sector, largely because modern clearances and restorations lowered ground levels and removed much of the later stratigraphy. Within this heavily truncated sequence, one of the few clear post-Roman features is the bottom of a well/shaft on the eastern side of the Arch, interpreted as a domestic refuse deposit (“butto”) containing abundant animal bone and a ceramic assemblage dated no later than the 14th century; the feature is plausibly connected with a small house documented in early-modern (16th-century) views of the area.

properties.c_notes:
The “discard pit” is located at the bottom of a stairwell inside the façade-tower of the complex rebuilt under Leo IV (847–855). In the 15th century, restoration works attributed to Cardinal Carrillo (1424–1434) included the closure of a ground-floor door, which effectively turned the lower part of the staircase into a convenient dumping space. The filling activity is dated —mainly by ceramics— to the late 15th century, while the final sealing/closure is placed around the mid-16th century, possibly linked to the establishment of the Augustinian community (1564). 


Archaeologically, the pit is composed of two main layers: US 3 and US 4. The entire fill is dominated by hay, within which ca. 6,000 desiccated (mummified) plant macroremains (35 taxa) were recovered, together with abundant food refuse and faunal remains. The assemblage is consistent with table/kitchen waste (cereals, pulses, fruits, vegetables/spices; plus shells, fish, birds, mammals), rather than a latrine-type deposit.

properties.c_notes:
During the 2011–2012 an excavation campaign was carried out within a former early-17th-century arched porch/portico, later subdivided into three rooms: Ambienti 1–3, belonging to the monastic complex. The work followed earlier investigations in the cloister/garden area and aimed to clarify the stratigraphic sequence in this service-facing part of the monument. 

Within Ambiente 3, an Imperial-period brick wall oriented NE/SW testifies the use of the area in the Roman period. The area appears to have remained open in the early Middle Ages, with beaten-earth surfaces, including one made with reused basalt paving stones (basoli) that is possibly connected to the Leo IV basilica phase.
Later, deposits and installations suggest a later medieval building-yard—likely associated with the 13th-century cloister works, before the area was finally reconfigured by the 17th-century portico. A key deposit from Ambiente 3, US 555 (charred timbers, many iron nails, tile fragments), has been interpreted as an accumulation of burnt roof-wood gathered on-site.

properties.c_notes:
URLS F15 is a deciduous oak (Quercus) specimen from Lingua d’Oca (Fiumicino), described as a wooden pile embedded in a light-grey clay layer in the coastal area west of Rome near the Tiber delta; the context is noted as marshy until modern reclamation (1925), with traces of Roman-age drainage also reported. 

The specimen is singled out as the oldest successfully genotyped oak examined in Deguilloux et alii 2006 and yielded a chloroplast haplotype (“a”) that was then identified in nearby modern oak populations, supporting the interpretation that the timber used at Lingua d’Oca was locally sourced.

properties.c_notes:
In the western part of the excavation (Sector G), a small cereal storage feature was identified and interpreted as a silo: US 2358 (structure/cut) and US 2359 (fill). The preserved portion measures roughly 0.85 × 0.80 × 0.20 m and was cut into a grey-reddish pozzolana/tuff unit (“Villa Senni”). Although truncated at the top, the internal morphology (a depressed end, slightly curving sides, and what was interpreted as a short “slide” and an arched/curved element suggesting an entrance) led excavators to propose it belonged to a more complex, partly subterranean, “pouch-shaped” facility rather than a simple open pit. The fill yielded tens of thousands of carbonised cereal grains, dominated by hulled barley (Hordeum vulgare), emmer (Triticum dicoccum) and einkorn (Triticum monococcum), together with arable weeds—clear evidence for bulk storage and/or the burning of stored crops.

Bibliography: Anzidei et al. 2007a; Anzidei & Carboni (eds.) 2020. .

US 2362 is a shallow, oval combustion-related feature (c. 1.70 × 1.10 m, depth c. 0.05 m) recorded in Sector A and attributed to Ortucchio Phase III. The context is archaeobotanically exceptional: flotation recovered 14,697 cereal grains, with a crop spectrum dominated by einkorn and emmer, accompanied by hulled barley and minor components, plus small quantities of legumes and arable weeds. The concentration and composition were interpreted less as “ordinary hearth sweepings” and more as evidence for cereal-processing episodes (e.g., cleaning/dehusking and possibly parching/toasting prior to storage or consumption), with the hearth acting as the locus where processing by-products accumulated and were carbonised.

properties.c_notes:
US 215 (Sector D) is a large, deep, pit-like combustion installation (reported as c. 1.60 m wide and up to 1.20 m deep), with walls showing intense firing/reddening and a fill rich in charcoal and burned material. A key archaeobotanical signal is the recovery of numerous fava bean (Vicia faba) cotyledons; one cotyledon provided a radiocarbon date (LTL990A: 3935±60 BP, calibrated to the mid–late 3rd millennium BC), anchoring the context within Ortucchio Phase III. The combination of structure form and botanical content supports interpretation as a specialised feature linked to heating/processing activities (potentially including food processing), rather than a simple domestic fire spot.

Bibliography: Anzidei et al. 2007a; Anzidei & Carboni (eds.) 2020. .

properties.c_notes:
Canale Trasverso was an engineered transverse channel that connected parts of the harbour system with the river-side waterways (under strong river influence). 

Stratigraphically, it includes deltaic sands at depth and a long canal-filling sequence with silts/clays containing pottery, wood fragments and molluscs—consistent with repeated dredging and reworking within an active harbour–canal environment. 

Archaeobotanical evidence (plant macroremains) is richer than in PTS13: 10 depth-interval samples between ~8.60 and 4.60 m contained enough seeds/fruits for study. Non-seed macroremains include frequent Posidonia oceanica fibres and scattered wood/bark fragments (e.g., Pinus cf. sylvestris, Ulmus, Alnus, Quercus sect. suber), again consistent with mixed marine debris and fluvial transport and harbour-canal maintenance dynamics. 

Overall, PTS5 captures a canal environment where plant input reflects both local wetland vegetation and anthropic disturbance/consumption waste, with changing salinity/river influence documented by the integrated proxy studies. 

Bibliography: Salomon et al. 2012; Sadori et al. 2010; Mazzini et al. 2011; Pepe et al. 2013; Giardini et al. 2013.

properties.c_notes:
PTS13 is a sediment core taken inside the Portus archaeological area, in the inner docking zone (the darsena/dock linked to the Claudian basin and later integrated within the wider Claudian–Trajanic harbour system). The core records the transition from pre-harbour deltaic deposits to harbour infilling sediments, with a long sequence of silty clays that accumulated during the functioning and progressive silting-up of the dock area. 
Archaeobotanical evidence (plant macroremains) is sparse but informative: only 6 depth-interval samples between ~4.90 and 1.70 m yielded enough seeds/fruits for analysis, and a major timber horizon occurs between 3.60 and 2.90 m. 
The remains are consistent with a dock setting repeatedly receiving floating plant debris from both marine/coastal environments (Posidonia) and the fluvial–wetland mosaic around the Tiber delta, with periodic phases of quieter vs more energetic (flood-influenced) conditions also suggested by the associated microfaunal proxies.

properties.context_name: "Vano della ruota”(waterwheel room) and associated finds
properties.chron_orig: end 1st century AD - beginning 2nd century AD
properties.c_notes:
A wooden wheel was installed in a long, narrow service room in the southern part of the baths, an area repeatedly modified into Late Imperial times. Excavation showed that this “wheel room” re-used earlier masonry (including Late-Republican walls later refaced and heightened) and reached more than 3 m below the modern walking level, revealing deep features interpreted as groundwater-drainage works and even traces of a timber-lined rectangular structure plausibly connected with a well or earlier water-collection arrangement. The installation is interpreted as a water-lifting device drawing directly on the water table; in popular reconstructions for this building, the wheel could be powered by human traction (treadwheel), raising water toward an upper reservoir feeding the bath complex.

From the same stratigraphic context came wooden macro-remains connected both to the device itself and to other objects recovered together (tools, pins, and a small female statuette). The identified taxa are overwhelmingly deciduous oak (29 pieces) and, more rarely, silver fir (4 pieces), suggesting the deliberate selection of robust timbers for structural/mechanical components and associated artefacts.

properties.parent_context: Anguillara Sabazia - Mura de Santo Stefano (sacred)
properties.c_notes:
A ditch-like feature encircling the Main Building and from a well/cistern in the vestibule. 

During the British School at Rome excavations, west, north and south trenches were cut across this shallow circuit-ditch; carbonised plant remains (c. 350 g of seeds) were recovered from the latter two of these trenches, using by dry- and wet-sieving on contexts [345], [374], [379] and [450]. Associated pottery (including sparse glaze and vetrina) points to deposition in the 10th–11th centuries, and the excavators interpret the deposit as stored crops (for consumption and/or sowing) disrupted by a fire and subsequently scattered. The published identifications highlight a cereal-and-pulse package typical of early medieval agrarian storage: free-threshing wheat, barley, emmer/spelt-type wheats, and a substantial legume component dominated by broad beans, with minor pulses and arable weeds also present.

properties.context_name: well from Room A of the Domus
properties.c_notes:
The archaeobotanical assemblage comes from the intentional backfilling/obliteration of a well intercepted below the domus, in the S/W corner (within “Ambiente A”). The fill is described as a unitary operation, articulated into two main dumping episodes separated by deliberate levelling/sealing actions (including layers of roof-tiles), with a strongly ceremonial character inferred for the uppermost phase; overall, the deposit contains an exceptionally large amount of material (tens of thousands of fragments), dominated by tableware (especially bucchero), alongside faunal remains and other classes. Chronologically, the assemblage as a whole is treated as a major sample of Veii’s 6th–5th century BC material culture, while elements from the deepest part help frame the obliteration as occurring after the Roman takeover, in a mid-Republican horizon. 

The macro-remains include carbonised plant material and worked/charred wood, interpreted as either accidental input from local vegetation or deliberate deposition with symbolic/votive value, also in light of associated carpological and faunal evidence. Palynological comparisons support a reconstruction of a landscape composed of mixed deciduous woodland with evergreen sub-Mediterranean elements, and cereal cultivation (notably wheat and barley) at regional scale.

properties.context_name: Cd "Casa del Nostromo" (early production area, later cementery)
properties.c_notes:
Within the castle’s internal articulation, the Casa del Nostromo area is a particularly instructive “micro-palimpsest”: excavation, documenting Roman phases (including architectural elements and high-quality surfaces), followed by late-antique/early-medieval re-uses. Finally, an extensive medieval cemetery installed itself above earlier structural remains. 

The archaeobotanical evidence discussed is tied to an early medieval productive installation, interpreted as a grain-roasting oven (forno per tostatura del frumento) set against earlier masonry and associated with a stratified sequence that includes a late-6th-century (post-560 AD) beaten surface and overlying activity/deposition connected to the oven’s use and disuse. Botanical sampling covered multiple stratigraphic units (26) and yielded hundreds of charred macroremains (seeds/fruits) dominated by cereal processing—especially free-threshing/naked wheat, with barley and smaller quantities of legumes and other food plants—consistent with an on-site chaîne opératoire of cleaning/roasting/handling crops in the early medieval occupation of the castle area.

Bibliography: Enei et alii 2013

properties.c_notes:
The 2002–2004 excavations exposed a an Egyptianising tomb–temple complex connected with the divinised Antinous (drowned in AD 130) wich comprises a walled sacred precinct with two opposed rectangular temples on podia, a central square foundation interpreted as the obelisk base, and a large exedra at the opposite end; the bedrock (tuff) was cut extensively both for foundations and for garden installation. 

A the deep rectangular-section planting trench running almost continuously around the two temples (c. 1.20 m deep and 1.50 m wide), cut into the tuff and filled with fertile soil to support large ornamental trees (probabily palms, in order to evoke an “Egyptian” setting). The same garden scheme included shallower parallel trenches near the obelisk base (interpreted as beds/planters) and a coherent irrigation system with lead pipes branching from a main conduit fed by a small cistern upslope—important for understanding how the planted setting was engineered, even if sampling concentrated on the deep trench.

properties.c_notes:
The 2002–2004 excavations exposed a an Egyptianising tomb–temple complex connected with the divinised Antinous (drowned in AD 130) wich comprises a walled sacred precinct with two opposed rectangular temples on podia, a central square foundation interpreted as the obelisk base, and a large exedra at the opposite end; the bedrock (tuff) was cut extensively both for foundations and for garden installation. 

In the area some antropic activity has been noted in the form of cuts in the tuff level wich shows a different (oblique) orientation. Some of these has proved to continue beneath the exedra’s foundations, therefore predating the Antinoeion’s construction (c. mid-2nd century AD). Among these earlier features is a rectangular pit (c. 3 × 3 m; preserved depth c. 0.30 m) containing a uniform soil layer with a charred plank trace along one side and an ash-rich patch with tuff chips and additional carbonised residues. The excavators interpret the ensemble, together with the surrounding quadrangular-section cuts, as evidence for cultivation/production installations belonging to the fundus of a nearby villa rustica predating Hadrian’s villa; a late Republican date (II–I century BC) is suggested by associated ceramic fragments and supported by radiocarbon dating of the charred wood studied archaeobotanically.

properties.c_notes:
Tomb 2 is an artificial rock-cut chamber tomb heavily affected by later agricultural truncation, preserving only a shallow portion of the structure. The surviving layout includes an eastern access area/vestibule (irregular/triangular in plan) sloping toward the chamber and connecting to it through a narrow opening. The burial evidence is highly disturbed and poorly preserved, with very deteriorated bone fragments and teeth indicating at least one adult individual; the associated assemblage is modest, including scattered pottery fragments and a flint arrowhead. 

Charcoal/wood macro-remains from Tomb 2 were identified as alder (Alnus sp.) and maple (Acer sp.), recovered within the funerary deposits.

properties.c_notes:
Grave 5 belongs to the group of small pit-type graves (3–7) cut into the cocciopesto floor after the main hypogeal/ossuary phase. Grave 5 is considered later than the other pit graves and was closed with bricks and mortar that disrupted the floor’s uniformity; part of the burial was removed when 18th-century cellar excavations cut through the stratigraphy.

Grave 5 is one of the pit-burials whose coffin wood survives as mineralized traces around nails and was identified as alder (Alnus sp.), in contrast with the poplar which seems to be used in the older crypt burial.

properties.c_notes:
Tomb 1 is a rock-cut hypogeum close to the church entrance, on the right aisle: an irregular rectangular chamber reached by a narrow stair, with an ossuary in the middle and two symmetric deposition platforms. The burial space was disturbed, but the excavation still documented multiple juvenile/child individuals and a set of devotional grave goods (e.g., rosary elements, a bronze crucifix, medals with saints).

The archaeobotanical finds belong to this funerary assemblage and to coffin/jewellery elements: poplar wood (Populus sp.) identified on nails/splinters from coffin remains; a necklace of birch wood beads (Betula sp.) threaded on wire; and an exceptional jasmine head-crown (Jasminum sp.), interpreted as part of funerary ritual display near children’s bodies.

properties.c_notes:
Under the church floor, in the W-SW area of the church, a conical pit-silo (US 164) was found. Below an upper arrangement interpreted as “alarii”-type elements composed of stones and reused ceramic fragments (US 162), were a fill (US 163) rich in carbonised botanical remains. It was probabily a storage silos belonging to a phase earlier than the church construction. The final infill then captured a concentrated snapshot of plant processing and disposal in the late 13th–early 14th century horizon. 

The assemblage is dominated by cereals and legumes, with associated weeds and fruit remains which seems consistent with mixed crop-processing residues rather than a single “clean” stored batch.

properties.c_notes:
A large well (or well-like installation) US 40 belongs to the same late 13th–early 14th century activity horizon beneath the church. Two abandonment/infilling units (USS 42 and 46) were sampled for anthracology, providing evidence for fuelwood selection and local woodland exploitation associated with the occupation that preceded (or immediately accompanied) the earliest church phase. The charcoal spectrum suggest opportunistic use of nearby mixed oak woodland resources.

properties.c_notes:
SE Bell-casting pit US –78 (associated deposit US 77)

One of two bell-casting pits belonging to the church’s building phase, the other one lying in the in the NW area of the Curch (US –109). The SE pit, here described, preserved internal firing features consistent with repeated casting operations. Within this operational setting, a charred stake from US 77 (a fill linked to the bell-casting installation) was analysed as part of the anthracological study. 

The stake was identified as an oak with ring-porous wood, probably Quercus sect. Cerris, consistent with the use of robust, locally available timbers in workshop/structural elements connected with casting activity.

properties.c_notes:
Pit 181 is the most complex and stratified of the pits, with distinct depositional episodes spanning the late medieval / early Renaissance transition and anchoring the site’s phasing.

Early deposits — Medieval (pre-1390): the earliest layers of Pit 181 fall in the Early group (within c. 1150–1390), evidenced in part by the associated numismatic horizon for the earliest deposits. 

Main filling — Renaissance (post-1390; “Main phase” ~c. 1390): the principal backfill belongs to the site’s major clearance episode, tightly dated by coins/seals to shortly after 1382 and plausibly within a decade of 1390; it is archaeologically linked to other pits of this phase (notably 4 and 9). 

Latest deposits — Renaissance (~c. 1400?–1436?): these additions belongs to a distinct layer, following the one just mentioned but still prior to the start of Vitelleschi’s palace works (1436).

Bibliography: Clark et al. 1989. "The Food Refuse of an Affluent Urban Household in the Late Fourteenth Century:
Faunal and Botanical Remains from the Palazzo Vitelleschi, Tarquinia (Viterbo)". In: Papers of the British School at Rome , 1989, Vol. 57 (1989), pp. 200-321.

One of the pits demonstrably filled concurrently with Pit 181 (and Pit 4) during the major late-14th-century clearance. It belongs to the Main group (labelled ~c. 1390) and is part of the same corridor/backyard system behind the proto-palace—sealed before/around the creation of the narrow street between Areas D and A3. 

Pit 9 was very rich in finds and ecofacts, with numismatic evidence anchoring its chronology. Coins finds in the pits places the filling shortly after 1382 and very likely around c. 1390, with no coins later than 1400 supporting a short time-window for deposition.

properties.c_notes:
The so-called "Tincu House" is the best-known excavated residence in Area B and represents a Mid-Republican urban dwelling inserted into Gabii’s later city fabric. Archaeologically, it is crucial because it preserves both standing architectural logic (a large townhouse plan) and the subfloor stratigraphy that explains how such a building was inserted into a pre-existing urban landscape—through major levelling and the management of earlier deposits. 

Ceramic and stratigraphic analysis place the initial construction (Phase 1) broadly between the second quarter and the middle of the 3rd century BC, after substantial levelling operations that incorporated residual earlier materials. The house then remained in use for roughly two centuries, undergoing modifications across subsequent phases. It is then a long-lived domestic investment mirroring, changing needs and the wider reorganisation of the city in the Republican period.

The cremated remains were collected in a column-krater (cratere a colonnette), and the tramite also yielded evidence for ritual deposition of goods—most notably a bronze strigil placed as a personal, status-marked item within the passage area rather than inside the niche itself.

(a) SU 27 (sediment context), 
(b) an additional sediment sample labelled N.D. 
(c) the filling of “Vase #1” (a ceramic vessel context).

properties.c_notes:
The “West Well” belongs to the same infrastructural/ritual system as the South Well and was likewise built in tuff blocks around 450–440 BC near Temple A. Its bottom lay at about 4 m depth, cut into an organogenic limestone lens interbedded within the clay. As with the South Well, excavation proceeded by 10 successive cuts, grouped into three main strata marking different moments in the well’s closure; the deeper Stratum III (cuts 5–10) contained the main concentration of preserved plant remains and had a thickness of about 2.50 m in the West Well.

properties.c_notes:
The excavated Early Imperial garden was organised on artificial terraces created by cutting earlier deposits and retaining them with concrete walls (Augustan Phase 3.1). Across these levels, archaeologists recorded planting trenches and discrete planting holes arranged in regular patterns parallel to the terrace walls, often with tuff fragments placed at the bottom for drainage and to prevent waterlogging. 

In the main planting episode relevant to the sampled material (Tiberius–Caligula, Phase 3.2), the layout includes circular and square planting holes (roughly 0.05–0.20 m wide and 0.10–0.25 m deep), set singly or in double rows about 0.8–1 m from the terrace walls; tighter clusters of smaller holes close to some walls suggest differentiated planting (e.g., edging or low shrubs versus larger specimens). This phase is also linked to an irrigation system using lead pipes, implying managed watering for ornamental and/or productive plants within a highly curated garden design.

properties.c_notes:
One particularly diagnostic garden installation of Phase 3.2 is a flower bed equipped with ollae perforatae: perforated ceramic pots set into the soil to hold plants while improving drainage and root aeration. In the ENPAM sector, multiple ollae perforatae were documented within a defined bed, alongside other container solutions (e.g., broken amphorae reused as flower pots) that point to intensive horticultural management and possibly the display/propagation of selected ornamentals or shrubs in a controlled substrate. 

These pots are central to the archaeobotanical programme: the published study explicitly ties many analysed sediments to the fill of smaller planting holes and to the ollae perforatae themselves, meaning that this “plant-pot area” provides a tightly contextualised window onto what was actually being cultivated (and how) during the Tiberius–Caligula redesign of the garden.

The hut yielded a limited but informative set of plant macro-remains, likely carbonised in connection with the fire that destroyed the structure. The published list includes cereals (emmer and einkorn, barley, and Triticum aestivum), durum wheat, legumes, and a small number of grape seeds—evidence consistent with a mixed agro-pastoral economy and with storage/processing of staple crops in (or near) domestic space.

properties.c_notes:
Charcoal recovered from the burnt posts associated with the hut’s postholes (both within the structure and along its perimeter) was identified as oak (Quercus sp.). This points to the deliberate selection of a hard, durable timber for the vertical load-bearing elements of the building (posts and principal supports), consistent with the need to anchor the roof and withstand long-term structural stress.

Bibliography: Celant, De Santis, Merlo & De Grossi Mazzorin 1998, Una casa dell’età del Ferro: la capanna di Fidene; “Una capanna dell’età del Ferro: archeologia sperimentale a Fidene”, Scuole Musei in Comune Roma (web resource).
properties.bibliography: Celant, A.,_De Santis, A._Merlo, R.,_De Grossi Mazzorin, J.,_1998_Fidene: una casa dell'Età del ferro. Mondadori Electa_1-47

properties.c_notes:
Wood remains attributed to horizontal components—explicitly including the walkway/boarding set on the bench in front of the entrance—were identified as elm (Ulmus sp.). In the publication this is interpreted as a functional choice: elm is described as comparably resistant but more flexible than oak, making it well suited to elements that had to “work” under movement and bending (walkways, boards, and other horizontals).

Bibliography: Celant, De Santis, Merlo & De Grossi Mazzorin 1998, Una casa dell’età del Ferro: la capanna di Fidene; “Una capanna dell’età del Ferro: archeologia sperimentale a Fidene”, Scuole Musei in Comune Roma (web resource).
